name: Archimedes’ hydrostatic equilibrium
description: Geometric treatment of fluid equilibrium and floating bodies.

impact.note: New quantitative understanding of buoyancy used by scholars and engineers in several civilisations; hydrostatics as a line of work grew from it.

date.label: 3rd century BCE
date.basis: Broad composition range based on Archimedes’ approximate lifetime, not a precise date of either treatise.

events.statement: On Floating Bodies developed geometric conditions for fluids and floating solids in equilibrium.

evidence.supports: Identifies the work and its treatment of equilibrium.
Places Archimedes in the third century BCE.

contributions.resource: Developed or authored the described account.

evidence.supports: Identifies the work and its treatment of equilibrium.

date.label: 10th century CE
date.basis: Date of the surviving manuscript copy, not composition.

events.statement: A tenth-century Greek manuscript preserved part of On Floating Bodies, including Book I.1–2.

evidence.supports: Dates the manuscript and identifies the folio text.

date.basis: Year of the source-bounded episode, not necessarily invention.

events.statement: William of Moerbeke translated a Greek copy of On Floating Bodies into Latin in 1269.

evidence.supports: The museum identifies the 1269 translation and its Greek sources.

contributions.resource: Translated the treatise into Latin from Greek in 1269.

evidence.supports: The museum identifies the 1269 translation and its Greek sources.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest dated source-bounded episode in this record, not a claim of worldwide priority.

caveats: The work was composed long before the surviving tenth-century copy and medieval translation. Treatise attribution and dating remain historical estimates; do not equate anachronistic vector-force terminology with the original presentation.

research.note: Chronology distinguishes composition or formulation from later surviving textual witnesses. Independent review checked the event dating and scope against the cited work, historical source, edition metadata or modern translation, as applicable.
